content: Six respondents were asked to provide additional information. Five of them confirmed that exclusive breastfeeding was promoted, but feeding practices were inconsistently assessed, often relying solely on self-reporting. The investigators assumed that some mothers exclusively breastfed for the recommended 5 to 6 months, while others introduced additional fluids, milk, or solids alongside breastfeeding, a practice known as mixed feeding. None of the studies disaggregated HIV transmission rates based on exclusive breastfeeding versus mixed feeding among mothers receiving lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART). Out of 18 cohort studies, only four provided estimates of HIV-free survival by feeding type, and only one of these also reported HIV transmission rates by feeding type. Another study compared cumulative transmission rates among children who were either formula-fed from birth, breastfed for less than three months, or breastfed for three months or longer. Three studies compared transmission or death rates between breastfed and formula-fed (replacement-fed) infants, and one study separately reported HIV-free survival for children who were mixed-fed and those who stopped breastfeeding early. Eight studies provided data on HIV-free survival or transmission and mortality rates from birth, while other studies excluded deaths and HIV transmission occurring in the first days or weeks of life, reporting only postnatal rates. A meta-analysis using a random-effects model was conducted, but due to significant clinical and methodological heterogeneity in the dataset, the authors cautioned against overinterpreting the results. Pooled estimates of HIV-free survival at 12 and 18 months were slightly higher for infants whose mothers received lifelong ART compared to those whose mothers received ART only up to six months postnatally. However, the data from individual studies were difficult to interpret due to heterogeneity and wide confidence intervals, particularly in studies with shorter ART durations. Generally, HIV-free survival estimates were equivalent or higher for infants of mothers receiving lifelong ART compared to those receiving ART for a limited period up to six months postnatally. However, the range of individual study estimates and confidence intervals could not be directly compared, as not all studies reported outcomes at both 12 and 18 months. The Guideline Development Group agreed that longer durations of ART for mothers are associated with greater HIV-free survival for young children. Four studies provided estimates of HIV-free survival by feeding modality, with three reporting higher HIV-free survival among breastfed infants compared to formula-fed infants. All studies were graded as low or very low quality due to their observational design and issues of indirectness. The authors urged caution in quoting pooled estimates due to heterogeneity. HIV transmission rates at six, nine, and 12 months among infants born to women receiving ART were summarized, but the data were limited by variability in study designs and reporting. Eleven studies were identified for analysis, including four cohort studies nested within randomized controlled trials. In all studies, mothers initiated ART before or during pregnancy and continued it until at least six months postnatally, in line with WHO recommendations at the time. Eight of the 11 studies followed the recommendation of using ART to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV during pregnancy and breastfeeding cessation at around six months postnatally. Three studies provided lifelong ART for all women, and one study provided lifelong ART only for women eligible for treatment under WHO guidelines. Most studies advised mothers to exclusively breastfeed their infants with rapid weaning after six months, while two studies recommended continued breastfeeding until 12 months. No study provided transmission rate estimates based on feeding type (exclusive versus mixed feeding), although two studies reported the feeding practices of infants who were found to be infected. Six studies reported overall HIV transmission rates (including peripartum and postpartum) at six months, while six others provided estimates of postnatal transmission between 4–6 weeks and six months, excluding peripartum infections diagnosed before 4–6 weeks of age. Seven studies provided information on transmission at 12 months, with five reporting overall transmission rates. All studies were rated as very low quality due to observational design, indirectness, inconsistency, and/or risk of bias. Despite substantial statistical heterogeneity between studies in each pooled estimate, the systematic review provided evidence of reduced postnatal HIV transmission risk under maternal ART. The analysis projected 24-month HIV-free survival among HIV-exposed, uninfected infants when varying three key parameters: the relative risk of infant and child mortality associated with replacement feeding compared to exclusive breastfeeding, setting-specific neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality rates, and the duration of maternal ART use during breastfeeding (as a proxy for retention in care and medication adherence). The analysis found that when the additional mortality risks associated with replacement feeding are high (e.g., in settings with contaminated water supplies or during diarrheal outbreaks), longer durations of breastfeeding (24 months or more) improve 24-month HIV-free survival if maternal ART is consistently available. When replacement feeding risks are lower, shorter breastfeeding durations (12–24 months) result in the highest rates of HIV-free survival, provided maternal ART is consistently available. The difference in HIV-free survival between 12 and 24 months of breastfeeding is minimal (<1%) as long as women continue ART throughout breastfeeding. However, if mothers stop ART before ceasing breastfeeding, the 24-month HIV-free survival of their children decreases dramatically due to high HIV transmission risks. In such scenarios, HIV-free survival is even lower if mothers do not breastfeed at all. The authors concluded that the 12-month breastfeeding duration recommended in the 2010 WHO HIV and infant feeding guidelines maximizes infant HIV-free survival at 24 months in many settings, even when replacement feeding risks or mortality rates are low. If programs in low-risk settings recommended 24 months of breastfeeding instead of 12 months, the anticipated reduction in HIV-free survival would be small (<1%), provided women continue ART throughout breastfeeding. In high-risk settings, breastfeeding for 24 months improves HIV-free survival. In all scenarios, ART adherence throughout the breastfeeding period is critical to improving infant HIV-free survival. The evidence suggests that breastfeeding may improve growth and non-HIV infection outcomes for HIV-exposed infants. Extended antiretroviral drug prophylaxis does not appear to increase the risk of adverse growth or non-HIV infections compared to short-course prophylaxis. However, earlier cessation of breastfeeding among HIV-exposed infants whose mothers received ART was associated with dietary deficiencies and reduced growth velocity in female infants, though it was unclear whether these effects were due to early breastfeeding cessation or other HIV-related factors. A survey of national health authorities in 22 priority countries of the Global Plan found that most countries recommend breastfeeding for mothers living with HIV while providing ART. The findings were presented to the Guideline Development Group and considered in their deliberations. The majority of the group agreed that the benefits of recommending breastfeeding for 24 months or beyond outweighed the risks of HIV transmission, provided maternal ART adherence is high. However, in settings where health systems do not reliably provide ART or where maternal adherence is inconsistent, the potential for HIV transmission increases.
